xfinity ⌁ reimagined
Unofficial redesign concept · not affiliated with Comcast

Feature-complete, experience-scattered.

The Xfinity app holds 4.3 stars across 1.4M ratings — proof of real capability, with user feedback pointing to one consistent opportunity: findability. Every feature exists; the experience is spread across five tabs, four outage surfaces, and role-gated navigation that silently disappears. This is a working prototype of a simpler structure, plus the map, audit, and requirements behind it.

What changed, and why

The current app is five tabs, an assistant, and forty-odd features that overlap. The redesign is four tabs where each answers exactly one question, with the assistant as a layer over all of them.

Status before navigation

The first thing on Home is whether your service works — a glowing gauge computed from gateway telemetry, the number-one reason anyone opens an ISP app. Billing, appointments and actions stack below it. The old Overview led with a greeting and a billing card.

Try · flip "Simulate an outage" below the phone
One outage surface, not four

Today the outage story spans an in-app banner, a separate outage map, SMS opt-in, and a credit request through the Assistant. Here it's a single screen: live timeline, map, text updates, and the credit applied automatically — stated, not requested.

Try · tap the outage banner on Home
WiFi absorbs Home

Cameras, thermostats and "modes" are network devices to a user, not a separate product line. Merging the WiFi and Home tabs into one Devices model removes a whole tab and the "which tab is my camera in?" question.

Try · WiFi tab → Devices → Pause
Sales is labeled, never disguised

Upgrades live in one clearly-marked Explore card with the full price shown before anything changes — the "Change speed" flow is your reference screenshot rebuilt as a native screen.

Try · Plan tab → Faster speeds
Roles inform instead of vanish

Today a Viewer simply has no WiFi or Home tab — the app looks broken. Here every role sees the same map; locked areas are dimmed and say who holds the keys.

Try · switch "Viewing as" to Viewer
Assistant is a layer, not a destination

It answers in place and deep-links to the exact screen — ask about the bill, land on the bill. It's also the app's universal search.

Try · the ✦ button → "Internet feels slow"

The outage night — an emotional arc, before and after

Same event, same repair time, same customer. The only variable is the app. The current experience loses trust twice: once while the customer hunts for answers, and again three weeks later when the credit has to be asked for. The redesign converts the same bad night into a demonstration that the company has it handled.

Current-app audit

Where the friction comes from

Sourced from Comcast's own support documentation, the App Store listing, and forum threads. The app isn't missing features — it's missing a point of view about where each feature lives.

4.3★
App Store rating — a strong base to build on
1.4M
Ratings — enormous, engaged user base
5 + 1
Tabs plus a floating Assistant — six navigation ideas
4
Surfaces in the outage journey (app, map, SMS, chat)
5
Roles that each render a different app

Surfaces per job — the overlap, measured

How many places in the app claim the same job. Magenta is today; green is the redesign. Every job collapses to one owning surface — everything else becomes a deep-link.

Billing3 → 1
Troubleshooting3 → 1
Outage status4 → 1
Device control2 → 1
Upgrades & offers4 → 1

Everything is there. Finding it is the work.

The consistent theme across recent user feedback: capability isn't the gap — findability is. Closing the distance between what the app can do and how quickly people can do it is the opportunity this redesign takes on.
Tab 01

Overview

A landing page with no thesis: greeting, billing, news feed, appointments, a store finder, and the outage banner all compete. Billing here duplicates Account; the Assistant entry duplicates the floating one.

Verdict — rebuild as status-first Home; keep bill glance and appointments, drop the feed and store finder below the fold
Tab 02

Services

Half service management (usage, lines), half storefront (add a line, change data plan, international passes) with no visual boundary between them. Troubleshooting routes out to the Assistant.

Verdict — split: usage & lines become Plan; sales moves to a labeled Explore section
Tab 03

WiFi

The absorbed xFi app, and the strongest tab — network, devices, pausing, hotspots, advanced settings. Its sin is what it can't see: the smart-home devices one tab over. Hidden entirely from Viewers.

Verdict — keep as the anchor; absorb Home's devices into its device model
Tab 04

Home

Cameras, smart devices, security status, and modes — a second device list that overlaps WiFi's. To a user, a camera is just another thing on the network. Also hidden from Viewers.

Verdict — merge into WiFi; "modes" become schedules on the unified device list
Tab 05

Account

Identity and money, plus a third copy of billing and more upgrade surfaces. Mostly sound — it's the one tab whose question ("who am I, what do I pay?") is almost crisp.

Verdict — keep; make roles visible as a people list, host the single Bill screen
Layer

Xfinity Assistant

Persistent 24/7 chat and the front door for troubleshooting and outage credits. Powerful, but it duplicates destinations instead of linking to them — and the credit requires asking.

Verdict — keep as a layer; every answer deep-links, credits become automatic

Documented behavior per role. When a tab is absent rather than locked, users can't tell missing-by-design from broken — the design-systems conversation waiting to happen.

The redesign's answer: one app for every role. Locked cards stay in place, dimmed, labeled with who can open them — try the Viewer switch under the prototype phone.

The same lens, turned on the redesign

A redesign that only audits its predecessor isn't credible. This is the usability review of the prototype itself — every finding was fixed in the current build, and the fixes are traceable to the principle they serve.

FindingViolatesSeverityFix, live in the prototype
Speed changes were reachable by every role — Members and Viewers could open the tier picker, though only Primary/Manager may change plans.R-03 · P4HighRole gate on the Speed screen: non-Primary roles get "🔒 Plan changes — Mikel (Primary) can do this," and Explore dims with the same message.
Status changes and toasts were invisible to screen readers — the gauge verdict and every confirmation were visual-only.R-51HighThe gauge verdict chip and the toast are polite live regions; outage flips and confirmations now announce.
The speed test had two owners — a "Run a speed test" card on Home duplicated the one inside WiFi, the exact ×2 pattern the audit flags in the current app.R-02 · P3MediumHome's card became "Network health," a deep-link into WiFi — the single owner of the test.
Device filter chips were decorative — All / People / Smart home highlighted but filtered nothing, teaching users that controls lie.P2MediumThe filter acts on the device model: People shows phones and laptops, Smart home shows TV, camera, thermostat.
"Pay now" beside "Autopay on" read as a double charge — the two statements contradicted each other on the Bill screen.R-32MediumCopy is now "Pay early," the subline says "pays itself Sep 3," and the confirmation states autopay is skipped.
The "Pause" quick action was ambiguous — pause what? It read as a media control.P2LowRelabeled "Pause device."

Still on the watch list: the assistant button can hover over the last list item on shorter phones (mitigated with scroll padding, needs device testing), and the gradient hairlines and glow are decorative only — no state is ever encoded in them, per R-55.

Redesign spec

Principles & requirements

Five principles drive every screen in the prototype; the numbered requirements below them are the buildable contract. IDs are stable so screens, map nodes, and audit findings can reference them.

P1

Status before navigation

The app's first pixel answers "is my service working?" Everything else — bill, visits, offers — queues behind that answer. During an outage the whole Home screen reorganizes around it.

P2

One question per tab

Home: what needs me? WiFi: my network and what's on it. Plan: what am I paying for and using? Account: who are we and how do we pay? A feature that answers two questions is two features.

P3

One address per feature

Nothing lives in two tabs. Cross-references are links, not copies — the bill card on Home opens the Bill screen owned by Account. Duplication is how navigation debt accumulates.

P4

Roles inform, never vanish

Every role sees the same map. Locked areas are visibly locked with the owning role named. A Viewer's app looks like everyone's app — just with keys they don't hold yet.

P5

Service and sales, separated

Offers live in labeled Explore surfaces, opt-in, with the full post-change price shown before commitment. A support flow never ends in an upsell.

Traceability — every requirement serves a principle

A requirement that serves no principle is scope creep; a principle with no requirements is a poster. Each dot below is at least one numbered requirement in the sections that follow.

Requirement groupP1 · Status firstP2 · One questionP3 · One addressP4 · Roles informP5 · Sales separate
Information architecture · R-01–03
Home & outage · R-10–13
WiFi & devices · R-20–23
Plan, billing & sales · R-30–34
Assistant · R-40–42
Accessibility & craft · R-50–55

Information architecture

R-01

Four bottom tabs — Home, WiFi, Plan, Account — with the Assistant as a floating layer, never a fifth tab.Collapses today's 5+1 model; WiFi absorbs the Home tab's devices (P2, P3).

R-02

Every feature has exactly one owning screen; all other appearances are deep-links.Eliminates the ×2/×3/×4 duplication mapped in the Screen map (P3).

R-03

All roles render identical navigation; gated features show a lock state naming the required role, with a one-tap "ask the Primary" request.Replaces tab-absence for Viewer/Guest (P4).

Home & outage

R-10

Home opens with a connection-status object (gauge + verdict) computed from gateway telemetry, above all other cards.P1. Healthy state shows speed and device count; degraded states name the cause.

R-11

The entire outage journey — live repair timeline, affected-area map, SMS updates toggle, and credit status — is one screen, reached from one banner.Replaces the 5-hop, 4-surface flow (app → details → map → SMS → chat).

R-12

Outage credits are applied automatically and stated ("Credit already applied"), never requested through chat.The single highest-leverage trust move in the app.

R-13

During an outage, Home demotes the status gauge to "Service interrupted" and promotes the outage banner to the top slot; the hotspot finder is surfaced as the fallback connectivity path.

WiFi & devices

R-20

One device model spans phones, TVs, cameras, and smart-home hardware, filterable by All / People / Smart home; pause, prioritize, and schedules act on any of them.Merges the WiFi and Home tabs' duplicate device lists.

R-21

Network credentials support show/hide, QR share, and a separately toggled guest network on one screen.

R-22

Cameras and Advanced Security appear inside WiFi as device-level cards with live-view and per-device history; "modes" become schedules attached to device groups.

R-23

Device filter chips (All / People / Smart home) act on the single device model — a filter that highlights without filtering is a defect, not a style.Added by the prototype self-review; live in the Devices screen.

Plan, billing & sales

R-30

Plan shows internet + mobile with real-time usage meters per line; nothing on this screen is a purchase surface.

R-31

Speed changes use the tier-picker pattern (the reference screenshot, rebuilt native): compare tiers, see "good for" guidance, and the full new monthly total — taxes in — before any Review step.P5. No change commits without an explicit review screen.

R-32

One Bill screen owns amount, due date, autopay, payment, "what changed vs last month" (credits called out), and 24 months of statements.Replaces three billing surfaces (Overview card, Account section, Assistant answers).

R-33

All offers live under an "Explore" label with dashed-border styling distinct from service cards; entering an offer flow is always opt-in.

R-34

When autopay is on, the manual payment action is labeled as paying early, the subline states when autopay runs, and the confirmation says the scheduled payment is skipped — a bill screen never implies a double charge.Added by the prototype self-review.

Assistant

R-40

The Assistant doubles as universal search: every screen, setting, and help topic is reachable by asking.

R-41

Assistant answers resolve to deep-links into owning screens ("bill is lower" → Bill; "feels slow" → Devices), never to parallel chat-only flows.P3 applied to conversation.

R-42

The Assistant is outage-aware: during an incident it leads with status and the hotspot fallback before any troubleshooting script.

Accessibility & craft

R-50

All interactive targets ≥44pt; primary actions in the bottom half of the screen for one-thumb reach.

R-51

Status is never color-alone: gauges, pills, and banners pair color with a word ("Healthy", "60% used", "Interrupted").

R-52

Numbers align with tabular figures; money and data amounts always show their unit and period.

R-53

Reduced-motion honors the OS setting; ambient aurora, screen transitions and the status gauge fall back to instant states.

R-54

Status changes and confirmations announce through polite live regions — the gauge verdict and toasts are heard, not just seen.Added by the prototype self-review.

R-55

Decorative treatments — gradient hairlines, glow, grain, the ghosted brand mark — never encode state. Every state carries a text label a decoration-blind reader still gets.Added by the prototype self-review.

Roadmap

How it stays simple

A redesign that ships once regrows its complexity one "just add it to Overview" at a time. Three guards against that: a placement algorithm every future feature must pass, a rollout that sequences the risky moves behind the cheap ones, and metrics that catch drift before reviews do.

Where does a new feature live? — the placement algorithm

Run every proposed feature through this, in order, and stop at the first yes. If it reaches the bottom, it is not a new surface. This one diagram is the difference between an IA and a pile of screens.

Is it about whether service is working right now — status, incidents, appointments, what needs attention today?
Yes →
Homewhat needs me
No ↓
Does it touch the network or a device on it — credentials, pausing, cameras, security, schedules?
Yes →
WiFimy network
No ↓
Is it about what you pay for or how much you use? (If it's an offer: it goes inside Explore, labeled, opt-in.)
Yes →
Planwhat I pay for
No ↓
Is it identity, people, or money mechanics — profiles, roles, statements, settings?
Yes →
Accountwho we are
Still no ↓
Then it is a conversation, not a surface. It becomes an Assistant answer that deep-links to an existing screen — or it doesn't ship. The sixth tab is never the answer.

Rollout — cheap trust first, hard plumbing later

Sequenced so every phase ships user-visible value on its own, and the scariest migration (removing a tab) happens only after behavior data proves the new paths carry the load.

Now · 0–3 months

Copy & consolidation

  • Locked, not vanished: role-gated areas render dimmed with the owning role named — pure client work, kills the "app looks broken" state
  • One outage screen: fold details, map and SMS opt-in into a single surface behind the existing banner
  • One Bill owner: Overview and Services billing cards become deep-links into Account's bill
  • Copy fixes: "Pay early" with autopay, price-before-review on upgrades
Risk: low — no data migration, no tab changes. Pure navigation and copy.
Next · 3–9 months

The merge & the credit

  • WiFi absorbs Home: one device model spans network + smart home; old Home tab redirects with a one-time "your cameras moved here" moment
  • Automatic outage credits: the billing-system integration — the hardest dependency and the biggest trust payoff
  • Assistant deep-links: answers resolve to owning screens instead of parallel chat flows
Risk: medium — device-model unification and a billing-policy change need cross-org buy-in.
Later · 9–18 months

Status-first & cleanup

  • The gauge: Home rebuilt around live gateway telemetry — status before navigation
  • Universal search: every screen and setting reachable by asking the Assistant
  • Demolition: retire duplicated surfaces and the old five-tab shell once redirect traffic falls under 5%
Risk: gated — demolition waits on the usage data, not the calendar.

How we'd know it worked

Four numbers, each tied to a principle. The review-sentiment metric keeps the work honest about the thing users feel most directly: how easy the app is to navigate.

Time to answer "is it down?"
< 2s from ~35s
Outage support contacts
−40% per incident
Top-5 jobs, unassisted success
≥ 90% 22→10 taps
